claims.text: The studied alloy has composition Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Slow cooling of this alloy produces a complex microstructure containing multiple crystalline phases.
The phases formed under slower cooling are primary non-eutectic phases.
Faster cooling reduces the number of crystalline phases, while very rapid melt-spinning can produce an amorphous structure.
The alloy exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization or solidification sequence whose transformation temperatures depend on cooling rate.
The proposed intervention is reheating at more than 200 °C/min followed by an approximately 30 s isothermal dwell at Tx - 5 °C.
The modified reheating schedule will suppress primary crystallization in the alloy.
The modified reheating schedule will increase amorphous retention and thermal stability.
The reheating protocol is applicable after either rapid cooling above 10^3 K/s or slower cooling near 10 K/min.
The cooling and reheating treatments are to be conducted in inert argon.
Rapidly traversing the crystallization-active temperature range reduces the time available for crystallization.
A 30 s hold at Tx - 5 °C minimizes atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility and limited time suppress the nucleation and growth of primary crystalline phases.
The modified schedule will decrease the intensity of the DSC crystallization exotherm relative to conventional continuous reheating.
The modified schedule will shift the crystallization onset temperature upward relative to conventional reheating.
The modified schedule will yield a higher amorphous fraction and less crystalline phase formation, as assessed by XRD and TEM.
Conventional lower-rate continuous DSC reheating without a dwell typically produces pronounced primary crystallization and a lower retained amorphous fraction.
The intervention is effective only within a narrow dwell-temperature window around Tx - 5 °C, and inaccurate Tx estimation or substantially different dwell temperatures may diminish the effect.
